Where it began

Nitish Kumar Reddy was born in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, on 26 May 2003. He was swinging a plastic bat by the age of five, and he spent his early years watching the senior players at the Hindustan Zinc grounds.

He was noticed in Under-12 and Under-14 matches by MSK Prasad, the former India player and selector, and went to train at the Andhra Cricket Association's academy in Kadapa. In the 2017–18 Vijay Merchant Trophy he had a season to remember: 441 against Nagaland from 345 balls, 1,237 runs in all at 176.41, a record for the tournament, and 26 wickets as well. It earned him the BCCI's award for the best Under-16 cricketer, the first time a player from Andhra had won it.

The player

He was Emerging Player of the Year in the 2024 Indian Premier League for Sunrisers Hyderabad, with 303 runs, and a few months later he made 74 from 35 balls against Bangladesh in only his second T20 international. That was enough to send him to Australia, where he made his Test debut at Perth on 22 November 2024 and top-scored with 41 in the first innings.

He kept getting within sight of fifty without quite reaching it, until the fourth Test of the series. He came in at number eight with India on 196 for 6, put on 128 with Washington Sundar and reached his first Test hundred, the first by an Indian number eight in Australia. In 10 Tests between 2024 and 2025 he made 396 runs at 26.40, with a best of 114, and took 8 wickets.

What made him special

A right-handed batter who bowled brisk medium pace, he showed in that Australian hundred how calm he could be with the score looking grim.

His bowling was more of a supporting act, his eight wickets costing 45.75 each. And his record has one happy oddity: one Test hundred and no fifties at all, as if he had decided that stopping halfway was a waste of a good start.

Away from the middle

He played his domestic cricket for Andhra and his franchise cricket for Sunrisers Hyderabad, who kept him on for the 2025 season. For a young man who began by watching other people play on a works ground, it was quite a journey.

And finally

In his first two Tests he was India's top scorer three times, a fine disregard for the idea that number eight is supposed to be the quiet end of the order.
